summary: Ages 7-8 (Y2/Y3): build genuine automaticity with single-digit sums and their related subtractions within 20, with a reconstructable strategy (make-ten, near-doubles) as a fallback for slips. Practice should be distributed, interleaved and low-stakes, treat subtraction as members of fact families, and stretch to deriving related facts to 100. A workable progression is: recall most sums while reconstructing a few by strategy; then recall all sums and the related subtractions (aiming for recall within about 3 seconds); then apply recalled facts instantly to derive facts to 100. The original row recommended an adaptive fluency game; strong alternatives (speeded retrieval practice, oral quick-fire, and a static fact-grid/strategy reference) are preserved here with their distinct purposes and limits.
misconceptions: Still counting on/back for facts that should be recalled, indicating incomplete automaticity.
Knowing sums but not the related subtractions (fact family incomplete).
Speed-without-accuracy under timed pressure, or anxiety suppressing recall.
Treating memorised facts as disconnected from strategies, so a forgotten fact can't be reconstructed.
Failing to use known facts to derive related facts to 100 (recomputing 18+5 from scratch).

activities.title: Personal fact grid: track recall vs counting, little and often
steps: Keep a grid of single-digit sums where each cell is a fact the child is practising (e.g. the row/column for crossing-ten sums like 8+7, 6+9).
Mark a fact as secure once it is recalled instantly (roughly within 3 seconds, no counting), and as 'still counting' when the child has to count on or pause.
Return frequently and briefly to the 'still counting' facts, mixed in with secure ones, rather than drilling one fact many times in a row.

When a fact slips, rebuild it aloud with a strategy — near-double (6+9 → 'double 6 is 12, plus 3 more is 15') or make-ten (8+7 → '8+2 is 10, then 5 more is 15') — then try it again cold a little later.
activities.insight: Automaticity is the fluent endpoint of understanding: instant recall for most facts, with a strategy to reconstruct any that momentarily slip, so recall stays connected to reasoning rather than brittle.

activities.title: Fact families: pull each subtraction from its addition
steps: For each secure sum, state the whole fact family: from 8+7=15, give 7+8=15, 15-8=7 and 15-7=8.
Practise subtraction prompts by first thinking of the matching addition: for 15-8, think 'what plus 8 makes 15?'
Use a fact-family triangle (15 at top, 8 and 7 below) to see all four facts come from the same three numbers.
activities.insight: Knowing a sum should give the related subtractions for free; subtraction within 20 does not need recounting from scratch.

activities.title: Derive to 100: show why knowing these by heart pays off
steps: Start from a recalled fact and derive related ones within 100: 8+5=13 → 18+5=23 and 38+5=43; 3+5=8 → 30+50=80.
Explain the link out loud: '3 ones plus 5 ones is 8, so 3 tens plus 5 tens is 8 tens, which is 80.'
Try a short chain of derivations from one known fact to feel the payoff of instant recall.
activities.insight: Secure recall of single-digit facts is the platform for fast mental calculation with larger numbers (the Tier C aim of applying recalled facts to derive facts to 100).

activities.title: Speeded retrieval practice (strong alternative): short, frequent, interleaved
steps: Work through short, mixed sets of single-digit sums and differences, aiming for near-instant answers (roughly within 3 seconds per fact).
Note which specific facts were not automatic so they can be targeted next time.
Keep sessions brief and frequent rather than one long high-pressure test.
activities.insight: Speeded retrieval is close to the target behaviour of 'knowing from memory' and is a useful practice and monitoring tool when kept low-stakes.

activities.title: Oral quick-fire warm-up (alternative): fast spoken recall
steps: Run a short quick-fire round of spoken sums and differences as a warm-up.
Mix additions with their related subtractions so fact families surface in conversation.
Ask the occasional follow-up: 'did you just know that, or did you build it?'
activities.insight: Spoken rapid recall builds fluency and lets a teacher hear strategy use directly.

activities.title: Static fact grid and strategy reference (scaffold)
steps: Keep a fact grid and a make-ten / near-doubles strategy card visible as a reference during practice.
Glance at it only to rebuild a slipped fact, not as the primary source of answers.
activities.insight: A reference anchor supports reconstruction but is a scaffold, not a driver of recall.

checkAnswer: 15, 7, 15, 7 — answered from memory or near-instant derivation (make-ten / near-doubles), with subtraction pulled from the related addition fact.
